title: Bud, Not Buddy (Selections & Bud's Rules and Things)
author: Christopher Paul Curtis
citation: Curtis, Christopher Paul. Bud, Not Buddy. Delacorte Press, 1999.

sections.heading: Rules and Things for Having a Funner Life

epigraph.quote: Bud Caldwell's Rules and Things for Having a Funner Life and Making a Better Liar Out of Yourself: Number 3—If you got to tell a lie, make sure it's simple and easy to remember.

paragraphs: It is 1936 in Flint, Michigan, at the height of the Great Depression. Ten-year-old Bud Caldwell has been an orphan since his mother died when he was six. Carrying his entire life in a battered cardboard suitcase—a blanket, a pair of spare socks, five smooth stones carved with mysterious numbers, and flyers advertising jazz legend Herman E. Calloway and the Dusky Devastators of the Depression—Bud survives on his wits.

To navigate a precarious world of harsh orphanages, abusive foster families, and street hustlers, Bud has formulated his own survival philosophy: 'Bud Caldwell's Rules and Things for Having a Funner Life and Making a Better Liar Out of Yourself.' These humorous yet heartbreaking rules reflect how a vulnerable child creates psychological structure, resilience, and boundaries when the adult world fails to protect him.

sections.heading: Hoovervilles, Jazz, and Finding a Home

epigraph.quote: When one door closes, don't worry, because if you keep moving, another door will open.

paragraphs: Escaping an abusive foster family who locked him in a hornet-infested shed, Bud sets off on foot toward Grand Rapids, convinced that the bandleader Herman E. Calloway is his long-lost father. Along the way, he encounters the reality of Depression-era America: shantytowns called 'Hoovervilles' where impoverished white and Black families share dandelion soup and communal fires, railroad police patrolling the boxcars, and compassionate labor organizers like Lefty Lewis who risk their lives distributing union flyers.

When Bud finally tracks down the Dusky Devastators at the Log Cabin club, he discovers the surprising truth: Calloway is not his father, but his grieving grandfather. Welcomed into the warm embrace of the band, handed a shiny brass recorder by Miss Thomas, and shown to his own room, Bud finally unpacks his suitcase. Remembering his mother's words—'When one door closes, another one opens'—Bud realizes that rules can guide your steps, but love and community give you a place to stay.
